When I first heard about Redis, I thought it was something only "big companies" needed.

I was wrong.

I added Redis to my FYP to solve two very real, very student-sized problems:

Problem 1 → My OTP flow was querying the database on every verification attempt. Redis replaced that with a 5-minute in-memory store that auto-expires. Clean. Fast. Simple.

Problem 2 → My timetable page made the same DB call over and over. The data hadn't changed. Yet the query kept running. Redis cached it. Problem gone.

What I didn't expect:

→ How easy it was to get started (seriously, 30 minutes to set up)

→ How much it changed the way I think about data  "does this need to live in the DB, or just in memory for now?

→ That caching isn't just about speed  it's about reducing load, cost, and failure points

Redis taught me something beyond the tool itself:

Not every problem needs a database. Sometimes fast memory is the right answer.

What tools did you learn during your Final Year Project that changed how you think?

Caching is not an optimization. It's a necessity , and Redis made me understand why.

During my FYP, I implemented Redis for two specific use cases:

𝟏. OTP Storage

Instead of writing OTPs to the database and querying them on verification, I pushed them to Redis with a TTL of 5 minutes.

Why this matters:

=> OTPs are temporary by nature. A DB record doesn't expire on its own.

=> Redis TTL handles expiry automatically. No cron job. No manual delete.

=> Verification became a single in-memory lookup instead of a DB round-trip.

𝟐. Timetable Caching

Timetables don't change every minute. But my app was querying the DB like they did.

Redis let me:

=> Cache the timetable data after the first fetch

=> Serve all subsequent requests from memory

=> Set cache invalidation when an update actually happens

The read pressure on my database dropped significantly.

Tools used: Node.js + ioredis client + Redis on the backend

If you're a student building your FYP  don't overlook caching. Your DB will thank you.

#Redis #Caching #BackendDevelopment #NodeJS #FinalYearProject #SoftwareEngineering #SystemDesign

In my Final Year Project (Digitized the University Bus timetable schedule with Real-Time Tracking of Buses ), I had two major bottlenecks:

→ OTP requests hitting the database every few seconds

→ Timetable data being fetched repeatedly on every page load.

Both of these were unnecessary reads. The data didn't change that often  yet every user request was going straight to the DB, creating a READ Pressue on the DB.

That's when I discovered Redis.

Redis is an in-memory data store , blazing fast, dead simple to use, and perfect for caching data that you read often but update rarely.

Here's what I did:

→ Stored OTPs in Redis with a TTL (time-to-live) of 5 minutes , auto-expiry, no manual cleanup needed.

→ Cached timetable data in Redis , served from memory instead of reading directly from the DB.

The result? My database pressure reduced alot. Response times dropped. And my app felt snappier.

If you're building anything with repeated reads , user sessions, configs, OTPs, frequently accessed data , give Redis a try.

It's one of those tools that makes you feel smart the moment you use it.

DAY-16 of levelling up my Backend Engineering Knowledge

Today I learned about HTTP 3 and how it improves modern web communication.

Unlike HTTP 1.1 and HTTP 2 which run on top of TCP, HTTP 3 runs on top of QUIC, which is built over UDP.

By using QUIC, HTTP 3 reduces connection setup time, improves performance in high latency networks, and solves the head of line blocking problem at the transport layer.

It also integrates TLS encryption by default and supports faster handshakes, including zero round trip in some cases.

Seeing the evolution from HTTP 1.1 to HTTP 2 to HTTP 3 makes it clear how much effort goes into reducing latency and improving reliability at scale.

DAY-14 of levelling up my Backend Engineering Knowledge

Today I learned the difference between HTTP 1.1 and HTTP 2 and why HTTP 2 was introduced.

HTTP 1.1 is text based and processes requests sequentially over a single connection, which can lead to head of line blocking. Even with persistent connections, each request still waits for the previous one to finish.

HTTP 2 is binary instead of text based and introduces multiplexing, which allows multiple requests and responses to be in flight at the same time over a single TCP connection.

It also supports header compression and server push, reducing overhead and improving performance.

Understanding this difference makes it clear how protocol evolution directly impacts latency, throughput, and overall backend efficiency.

DAY-11 of levelling up my Backend Engineering Knowledge

Today I learned about the UDP protocol and its tradeoffs.

UDP is a simple, connectionless transport layer protocol. It has no handshake, is stateless, and sends data without guaranteeing delivery or order.

Because of this, it offers low latency and minimal overhead, which is why it is commonly used in online games, live streaming, DNS, and real time communication.

The downside is that UDP has no built in reliability, no retransmissions, no congestion control, and packets can be lost, duplicated, or arrive out of order.

Using UDP means the application must handle these issues itself if reliability or ordering is required.

DAY-10 of levelling up my Backend Engineering Knowledge

Today I learned about the OSI model and how it explains the complete journey of data across a network using layers.

The model has seven layers. Physical handles raw bit transmission over cables and signals. Data Link deals with frames, MAC addresses, and local network delivery. Network is responsible for logical addressing and routing, like IP. Transport manages end to end communication, reliability, and flow control, such as TCP and UDP. Session handles connection management between systems. Presentation focuses on data formatting, encryption, and compression. Application is where protocols like HTTP, FTP, and SMTP live and interact with software.

Understanding what each layer is responsible for makes it much easier to reason about network issues and backend communication problems.

This gives a strong foundation before diving deeper into real world protocols and system design.

DAY 8 of levelling up my Backend Engineering Knowledge

Today I dove into the Publish Subscribe or Pub/Sub model. This is a massive shift from the point to point communication patterns I have been studying so far. It introduces a message broker into the mix which decouples the sender from the receiver.

I put this into practice by setting up RabbitMQ. I built a publisher that sends jobs to a queue and a consumer that listens for those jobs to process them. It was interesting to see the asynchronous nature of this setup. The publisher does not care if the consumer is online or how long it takes to finish the job it just drops the message and moves on.

Key takeaways from today:

The publisher and consumer do not need to know anything about each other. This makes the system much more flexible and easier to scale.

If the consumer is busy or goes offline the message broker holds the jobs in a queue until the consumer is ready again.

In my specific practical I noticed that while one consumer is processing jobs any other consumer that connects has to wait if they are competing for the same queue. This is a common way to handle load where you can add more consumers to share the work but only one gets to work on a specific message at a time.

This pattern is the backbone of distributed systems and microservices where different parts of an application need to talk without being tightly coupled.

DAY 7 of levelling up my Backend Engineering Knowledge

Today I explored Server Sent Events also known as SSE. This is a very interesting middle ground between the traditional request response model and full duplex WebSockets.

In an SSE setup the client establishes a long term connection with the server using a simple HTTP request. Once this connection is open the server can stream data to the client whenever it wants. Unlike WebSockets which allow two way communication SSE is unidirectional the data only flows from the server to the client.

Key takeaways from today:

Since it uses standard HTTP it works through most firewalls and proxies without any special configuration. If the connection drops the browser will automatically try to reconnect for you which is a huge plus for reliability. It is incredibly lightweight because it does not have the protocol overhead that WebSockets do.

It only allows data to flow from the server to the client. If the client needs to talk back it has to send a separate HTTP request. Most browsers have a limit on the number of open SSE connections you can have at once which can be a bottleneck for certain apps.

I find it fascinating how SSE is the perfect choice for things like live news feeds, stock tickers, or social media notifications where the user just needs to receive updates without necessarily sending data back in the same pipe.

DAY 6 of levelling up my Backend Engineering Knowledge

Today I moved from Short Polling to Long Polling to see how we can make the request-response cycle more efficient for real-time updates.

In Short Polling, the client keeps asking and the server often says nothing is new. Long Polling changes this. The client sends a request and the server hangs onto that request. It does not respond until it actually has new information or a timeout occurs. As soon as the client gets a response, it immediately sends another request to start the process over.

I modified my job status practical to see the difference. Instead of the server immediately returning the current progress, I implemented logic where the server holds the request in a pending state. Only when the background job is fulfilled does the server finally send the response back to the client.

Key takeaways from today:

It is much more efficient than short polling because it eliminates the constant noise of empty responses. 

The server only talks when it has something to say.

It feels much closer to real-time because the data is sent to the client the moment it is ready.

The server has to hold onto connections, which can be tricky to manage at high volume. 

It still follows the request-response flow, so there is still some overhead compared to a pure stream.

This was a great bridge to understand how we evolved from simple requests to more persistent communication.

DAY 5 of levelling up my Backend Engineering Knowledge

Today I explored Short Polling. While we usually think of the Request-Response model as a one-off interaction, Short Polling turns it into a repetitive loop to simulate real-time updates.

In this model, the client automatically sends a request to the server at fixed intervals, such as every 2 or 5 seconds, to check if there is any new data or a status update. The server responds immediately, even if nothing has changed.

I put this into practice by building a job status system. I created a submission route that adds a job to a dictionary and a status route that the client polls. To simulate a long-running process, I made the job progress by 10% every few seconds. The client keeps asking for the status until the job hits 100%.

Key takeaways from today:

Very easy to implement and works over standard HTTP without needing persistent connections like WebSockets. Good for non-critical updates where a small delay is acceptable.

It creates a lot of empty traffic. If the data hasn't changed, the server still has to process the request and send a response, which wastes resources. It is not truly real-time. The client only knows about a change after the next poll happens.

This practical helped me see exactly why this can be a bottleneck at scale and why patterns like Long Polling were created to solve the "empty response" problem.

DAY 4 of levelling up my Backend Engineering Knowledge

Today I took the theory of the Push model and put it into practice by building a real time chat application using plain #Nodejs and #WebSockets.

Instead of using high level libraries, I wanted to see how the connection management works at a lower level. I implemented this by maintaining an array of active connections on the server side. Every time a new browser tab opened, it acted as a unique client.

Key mechanics of the implementation:

When a new client connects, the server pushes a notification to every other active connection in the array to let them know someone new joined.

The server keeps a persistent list of all connected sockets. This is the heart of the Push model because it gives the server a direct line to every user.

When one client sends a message, the server iterates through the array and pushes that message to every other connected socket instantly.

Building this really highlighted the trade offs. While the real time speed is incredible, you can see how the backend has to work harder to keep track of every single open connection. If the array grows too large or connections drop unexpectedly, the management logic becomes much more critical.

DAY 3 of levelling up my Backend Engineering Knowledge

Today I looked into the Push communication model. This is a shift from the traditional way we think about the web where a client always has to ask for data first.

In the Push model, once a connection is established, the server can send data to the client whenever new information is available. The server takes the initiative. This is how we get real-time experiences like live sports scores, stock price updates, or instant messages.

Key takeaways from today:

Real-time delivery:

 Data reaches the client almost the instant it is available on the server. 

Lower latency:

 Since the client doesn't have to keep asking for updates, there is no delay between an event happening and the client being notified. Reduced bandwidth. It can be more efficient than polling because data is only sent when it actually exists.

Resource heavy:

 The server must maintain an open connection for every single client, which can strain memory and CPU as you scale to thousands of users. Connection stability:

 If a client has a poor internet connection and the link drops, the server needs a way to handle that reconnection and potential data loss. Complexity. Implementing a robust push system requires more complex backend logic compared to a simple request-response setup.

DAY 2 of levelling up my Backend Engineering Knowledge

Today I looked into the difference between synchronous and asynchronous workloads. Understanding when to use which is one of the most important decisions in backend design because it directly impacts how a user perceives the speed of an application.

In a synchronous workload, tasks are performed one after another. The system starts a task and waits for it to finish before moving to the next one. It is straightforward and easy to debug, but if one task takes a long time, the whole process gets stuck. This is usually what happens when you wait for a page to load after clicking a button.

In an asynchronous workload, the system starts a task and immediately moves on to something else without waiting for the first task to finish. The completion of that task happens in the background. This is essential for long-running jobs like sending a heavy email, processing an image, or generating a large PDF report.

Main takeaways from today:

Synchronous is great for simple operations where you need the result immediately to proceed.

Asynchronous is a lifesaver for keeping systems responsive. It prevents the backend from being blocked by slow operations.

Choosing between them is a tradeoff between simplicity and system efficiency.

DAY 1 of levelling up my Backend Engineering Knowledge

Today I spent time breaking down the Request-Response model. While it seems simple on the surface, there is a lot happening under the hood when a client and server talk to each other.

In this pattern, the client initiates a connection and sends a formal request. The server processes that request and sends back a response along with a status code. The most important thing to remember is that the client is usually in a waiting state until that data comes back.

Key takeaways from today:

The client always starts the conversation. The server cannot send data to the client unprompted in this specific model.

It is stateless by nature. In its purest form, each request is independent and doesn't know what happened in the previous one.

It is ideal for many web applications but can be inefficient if the client needs real-time updates without constantly asking for them.

Understanding this flow is helping me see why we sometimes need to move toward other patterns like Pub/Sub or WebSockets when the waiting time becomes a bottleneck.

There are mainly three types , and here’s how I understood them with a simple bus example:

==>Public Cloud

 Imagine a public bus , anyone can buy a ticket and use it.

 In the same way, a public cloud is shared by multiple users or organizations.

 It’s managed by cloud providers like AWS, Google Cloud, or Azure, and you only pay for what you use.

 Example: Gmail, Google Drive, AWS EC2 (public access and shared infrastructure).

==>Private Cloud

 Now think of a private company bus , only employees can use it.

 Similarly, a private cloud is dedicated to a single organization.

 It offers more control and security since the resources aren’t shared with others.

 Example: An enterprise hosting its own cloud on-premises using VMware or OpenStack.

==>Hybrid Cloud

 This one is like using both public and private buses depending on the need.

 A hybrid cloud combines both public and private environments, allowing data and applications to move between them as required.

 It provides flexibility , sensitive data stays private, while other workloads can use the public cloud for scalability.

 Example: A company using AWS for hosting its website but keeping customer records in a private on-premises server.

In short:

Public Cloud → Shared and scalable

Private Cloud → Secure and controlled

Hybrid Cloud → Best of both worlds

Day 1 of My Cloud Computing Journey ,Understanding Virtualization

Today I started my cloud computing journey by exploring the core concept that makes cloud possible ,"Virtualization".

Here’s what I learned in simple terms:

Virtualization means creating multiple virtual environments or machines on a single physical system. It allows one physical computer to act like many, each running its own operating system and applications independently.

The system on which virtualization runs is called the Host Operating System, and each virtual machine created on top of it is called a Guest OS.

At the center of it all is something called a Hypervisor , a software layer that manages and allocates resources between the host and the virtual machines.

There are two main types of hypervisors:

Type 1 (Bare Metal): Installed directly on the physical hardware. These are faster and used in data centers (like VMware ESXi, Microsoft Hyper-V).

Type 2 (Hosted): Runs on top of an existing operating system. Great for local testing (like VirtualBox or VMware Workstation).

Finally, I got a clearer picture of how this idea of virtualization evolved into what we now call Cloud Computing , where instead of creating virtual machines on our own computers, we rent computing power from cloud providers like AWS, Google Cloud, or Azure.

It was a solid start. Excited to continue sharing what I learn every day as I move forward in this journey.

Built a Cool App. Deployed It. Accidentally Invented a Time Machine.

Yesterday, I deployed a seemingly simple project.

 A user could add tasks, assign a date, and later filter those tasks by date.

 ==> On localhost: flawless.

 ==> On production: a mystery bug appeared.

A user reported that when they added a task at 8:00 PM, it was showing up in the database as 3:00 PM ,  a 5-hour time gap.

 Other users confirmed the same issue. I immediately opened VS Code, checked everything again , locally, it was still working perfectly.

So what went wrong?

I turned to the best senior developer we all secretly have  #ChatGPT , and started digging. Here's what I learned:

==> I was sending dates in ISO format

==> But the database (hosted on a server in a different timezone) was storing them as UTC

That was the gap. ISO + timezone difference = misaligned timestamps.

To fix it:

 ==> I converted the ISO datetime to UTC on the frontend before sending it to the database

And boom , issue resolved. The task now shows the correct time, no matter where it's saved or viewed.

Takeaway

==> Deployment isn't a destination , it's exposure to the real environment

==> Local testing doesn't account for timezone, latency, infrastructure, or edge cases

 ==> Production feedback is priceless — let real users interact with your work

Ships are meant to sail, not to rest at the docks.

 So ship your product , bugs and all , because the ocean will teach you more than the shore ever could.

Screw can be opened by a Hammer as well but we still open it with screw driver,

as knowing the right tool save us time , make the task easy and efficient.

As sir Mohammad Nauman once said in his videos:

“If you have a hammer and a screwdriver, knowing which tool to use where is the real trick.”

Sure, you can open a screw with a hammer — force it, break it, maybe even get the job done.

 But if you want it done efficiently, safely, and without future problems, you reach for a screwdriver.

I thought I had it all figured out. I realized it when I had to a task which was automatically send the reminders after some specific time.

Just a simple background task.

 Run every 5 minutes.

 Send the reminders.

 What could go wrong?

I reached for setInterval. It was fast, easy, clean.

 Minutes later, the feature was live. And it worked perfectly... for a while.

But then came the fire.

Random crashes.

 Duplicate entries.

 Unpredictable behaviors.

 Logs that made no sense.

The worst part? It only happened sometimes.

 Only in production.

 Only when I wasn’t watching.

That’s when I realized something painful:

==> setInterval doesn’t care if your app crashes. It doesn’t persist. It doesn't retry.

 ==> It runs in-memory, and once the server dies or restarts — it's gone.

 ==> Multiple intervals can accidentally stack up if you're not careful.

What I really needed was a cron job.

==> Cron jobs are built for reliability.

 ==> They run based on real time (not app uptime).

 ==> They survive restarts.

 ==> They don’t overlap unless you tell them to.

 ==> And they scale cleanly as your app grows.

I replaced the setInterval with a simple node-cron expression:

 0 */5 * * * * — every 5 minutes.

And just like that, the chaos stopped.

 No more race conditions.

 No more ghost processes.

 No more guesswork.

Lesson learned:

 Choose the right tool not just for now, but for what happens when you’re not looking.

If you’ve ever been burned by a background task…

 or spent hours debugging something that should have been simple…

 I know you’ll feel this one.

Let’s just say:

 I now respect time — both human and system time — a lot more than I used to.

Debounce vs Throttle –– Same Same, But Different 😂 ?

It took me several tutorials and a few hours with ChatGPT to understand this concept, but you'll understand it in just 3 mins.

--Debouncing:

Debouncing means delaying the execution of a function until a certain period of inactivity — for example, until the user stops typing.

Let’s say we want to search for a product from a large JSON object. We've passed the search keyword as a dependency in the useEffect hook, so the search function gets called every time the user presses a key.

--The problem?

 The function gets executed way more times than necessary, which leads to unnecessary rerenders and performance lags, unresponsive UI errors — especially if the JSON is huge.

--The solution — Debouncing:

 We delay the function execution until the user finishes typing. So instead of running on every keystroke, the function runs only once when the user stops.

This results in:

Fewer function calls

Which ultimately results in improved performance and smoother UI.

--Throttling:

On the other hand, throttling means calling a function at regular intervals not more frequently than a defined delay (like once every 300ms), even if the event keeps firing.

Let me give you a real example:

Imagine in an e-commerce project, we have a button that places an order. When clicked, the frontend sends a POST request containing:

Product ID, color, name, user ID, name, address, phone, email, payment info, quantity, notes, etc.

Now, while the backend is busy saving this data to the database, the user might click the button multiple times. This can:

-- Send duplicate requests

 -- Overload the backend

 -- Cause unexpected behavior or even crashes (if try & catch are not used intelligently)

One way to handle this is by throttling the button click handler allowing only one request every few milliseconds.

(Though a better solution might be disabling the button after one click, throttling can still help as an extra safety net.)

Another great use case is infinite scrolling (e.g., YouTube, Instagram, Facebook). If a user scrolls too fast, the app might fire tons of requests to fetch new data.

With throttling, we can limit how often scroll-triggered functions run — reducing backend load and improving performance.

So in a nutshell use debounce when you want to reduce unnecessary calls, and throttle when you need to control the frequency of actions.

Is JavaScript Compiled or Interpreted? The Answer Might Surprise You!!!

When working with programming languages, we often categorize them as:

1:Compiled Languages (C, C++)

2:Interpreted Languages (Python)

In compiled languages, a compiler translates the entire code into machine code before execution. The compiled program runs as a whole, making it faster but requiring compilation beforehand.

On the other hand, an interpreter reads and executes code line by line at runtime, making execution flexible but often slower compared to compiled languages.

What Makes JavaScript Different?

JavaScript does not fit strictly into either category. Instead, it uses a technique called Just-In-Time (JIT) Compilation.

Initially, JS interprets the code, just like an interpreter. However, it identifies frequently used parts of the code and compiles them into optimized machine code, just like a compiler. This compiled code is reused, avoiding repetitive interpretation and significantly improving execution speed.

How Does This Work?

Let's take an example:

Imagine a function that adds two numbers. When calling the function, we pass two numbers to be added.

Without JIT Compilation:

The JavaScript engine interprets the function every time it is executed.

With JIT Compilation:

The engine detects that the add function is used multiple times in the code. It compiles it into optimized machine code and reuses it for faster execution.

Why Does This Matter?

Various JavaScript engines, like V8 (Chrome, Node.js, MS Edge), SpiderMonkey (Firefox), and JavaScriptCore (Safari), use JIT Compilation to make JavaScript execution faster and more efficient.

This is what makes JavaScript unique—combining the best of both worlds (interpreted and compiled) to deliver better performance and speed.

How Web Workers Can Speed Up Your Website and Enhance User Experience?

Have you ever had a webpage freeze while :

-loading large datasets

-running complex calculations

-processing images? 

That lag happens because JavaScript is single threaded language ,which means  that  it handles everything i.e: UI updates, rendering, and logic on a single thread. When heavy tasks run on this same thread, the browser can become unresponsive.

To solve this, Web Workers were introduced in HTML5. They allow JavaScript to execute tasks in the background on a separate thread, preventing UI lag. Instead of slowing down your app, these tasks run independently, keeping the interface smooth and responsive.

How Do Web Workers Work?

Web Workers are basically background assistants, they take care of high computations while your main thread on which the UI or Javascript is being executed,  stays focused on user interactions. For example, if your app needs to parse a large JSON file or perform realtime data processing, a Web Worker can handle it without freezing the UI.

When Should You Use Web Workers?

1:Complex mathematical Formulas eg: finding largest prime number.

2:Reading/Writing large data from localstorage/Database

3:Processing Images/Videos etc.
